slides.title: Clarity, satisfaction and style
slides.source: Source: Riot Games, “So You Wanna Make Games??” Ep 1, Intro to Game Art.
slides.notes: The 16 px and 3:1 rule, the 40 ms and 700 ms delays, and the head ratios are illustrative. Saturation is computed with HSL. Palette is covered in the 2D art deck.
slides.picture: Eight things at game size with a count of those that read. A fast answer against a slow answer to a button press. The same scene in two palettes with their saturation. Three figures with growing head sizes.

can you tell what is going on
does it feel good to act

slides.title: Visual hierarchy and contrast
slides.source: Source: Riot Games, “So You Wanna Make Games??” Ep 1, Intro to Game Art; Chapter 6, Shader foundations, the flash-colour exercise (contrast ratio).
slides.notes: Attention share is size squared times contrast ratio, a simple stand-in. The contrast ratio formula and the 1.11 and 11.23 examples are from Chapter 6.
slides.picture: Attention shares for six objects sorted from most to least. Contrast ratios for three colour pairs. Six colours converted to grey by luminance. Two rows of circles showing strong and weak saturation contrast.

slides.title: Focus, rest and distance
slides.source: Source: Riot Games, “So You Wanna Make Games??” Ep 1, Intro to Game Art.
slides.notes: Checkerboard shades and ratios are computed from sRGB values; detail counts and the falloff constant 0.35 are illustrative inputs.

Survive smallest: pauldron, sword, scarf. Rule: 3 px on the thinnest side (illustrative).
Iconic elements are the features that still read when the character is tiny. Choose the wrong ones and the essence is lost.

Anatomy: where the bones and joints are decides how a creature can move. A joint gives reach that a rigid bar lacks.

slides.title: Before you call a piece of art ready
slides.source: Source: Riot Games, “So You Wanna Make Games??” Ep 1, Intro to Game Art; Riot Ep 2, Concept Art; Riot Ep 3, Character Art.
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Can a player tell what is happening at once, and does the game answer?
Where does the eye land first, and is that the most important thing?
Does the silhouette still read, filled black at game size?
Which constraint does this design solve, and what is the reference?
Did I show it early and ask a specific question about the goal?
Does the character read at the size it has in the game's real view?
Then say it exactly: a number, a size, a limit, not “make it better”.
